title: The Surface |X(s)|
intro: For most signals in engineering, X(s) is a ratio of polynomials. That means it is fixed by a handful of numbers: where its zeros and poles are, and one constant. This page shows how those few points shape the whole landscape, and how to read the height with a ruler.

blocks.text: Factoring into poles and zeros
Take the damped sine $x(t) = e^{-0.5t}\sin(1.5t)\,u(t)$. Its transform is
The denominator is zero where $(s + 0.5)^2 = -2.25$, that is at $s = -0.5 \pm j1.5$. Factor it and the transform becomes

In general, a rational transform factors as $X(s) = K\,\dfrac{(s - z_1)(s - z_2)\cdots}{(s - p_1)(s - p_2)\cdots}$. The $z_k$ are the zeros, where $X = 0$. The $p_k$ are the poles, where $X$ becomes infinite. $K$ is the gain. These numbers are all there is: a rational transform is its poles, its zeros and its gain. The same is true of the z-transform, as The Surface |X(z)| (#/math/z-transform/surface) explains.
For the damped sine, there are no zeros, two poles at $-0.5 \pm j1.5$, and gain $K = 1.5$.
Reading the height with distances
Because each factor $s - p$ is the vector from the pole $p$ to the point $s$, its size is a distance. So at any $s$,

blocks.tex: |X(s)| = |K|\, \frac{\prod_k |s - z_k|}{\prod_k |s - p_k|} = |K|\, \frac{\text{distances to the zeros, multiplied}}{\text{distances to the poles, multiplied}}

blocks.text: This turns reading the surface into measuring with a ruler. Put the point at $s = j1$ on the imaginary axis. Its distance to the pole at $-0.5 + j1.5$ is $|0.5 - j0.5| = 0.707$. Its distance to the other pole, $-0.5 - j1.5$, is $|0.5 + j2.5| = 2.55$. So

Slide the point up to $s = j1.5$, level with the upper pole. The near distance shrinks to $0.5$ and the far one grows to $3.04$, so $|X| = 1.5/(0.5 \times 3.04) = 0.986$. Past that, at $s = j3$, the distances are $1.58$ and $4.53$ and the height has fallen to $0.209$, which is $-13.6$ dB. The rule is: close to a pole, the height rises; close to a zero, it falls; far from everything, the distances change slowly and so does the height.

The viewer's step Reading |X| with a ruler writes out exactly this product for the probe point, with the distances to every zero and pole. The green lines in the s-plane panel are the zero distances and the dashed violet lines are the pole distances.

Leave Probe frequency ω at 1 and press Next step until the step Reading |X| with a ruler: it should quote the two distances, $0.71$ and $2.55$, and the value $0.83$ ($-1.6$ dB). Now drag Probe frequency ω to 1.5: the near dashed line shrinks to $0.5$, and the response panel's marker rises. Raise Tilt to about 85° to look straight down: the two poles are the two bright spots, at $\sigma = -0.5$ and $\omega = \pm 1.5$. The lower one at $-1.5$ is outside the probe's range, which only runs from 0 to 3, but its distance still counts.
What a pole does to the surface

Near a simple pole $p$, the factor $1/|s - p|$ dominates: $|X(s)| \approx \dfrac{c}{|s - p|}$ with $c$ the size of everything else, evaluated at $p$. For our damped sine, $c = 1.5/|{-0.5 + j1.5} - {(-0.5 - j1.5)}| = 1.5/3 = 0.5$. So the height is $0.5/d$ at distance $d$ from the pole: a spike with a funnel shape. At $d = 0.3$ it is $1.67$; at $d = 0.1$ it is $5$.

In decibels the spike is clipped at $+30$ dB, a height of $31.6$, which for this signal happens only within $0.016$ of the pole. The viewer computes the surface on a grid of points $0.15$ apart, and for these poles the nearest grid point is $0.05$ away, where the height is $10$, or $20$ dB: so in decibels the drawn peak stops short of the ceiling, and a vertical line from the floor to the top marks where the pole is. In the magnitude setting the surface is clipped at 5, which happens within $0.1$ of the pole, so there the grid points next to the pole are cut off at the top of the box. Neither is the true shape; the true surface goes to infinity at the pole.

A double pole, as for $t\,e^{-0.5t}u(t)$ with $X(s) = 1/(s+0.5)^2$, rises as $1/d^2$. In decibels that is twice as steep: at the same distance, the height in dB is doubled. At $s = 0$, for example, $|X| = 1/0.25 = 4$ which is $12.0$ dB, twice the $6.02$ dB of the single pole $1/(s+0.5)$ at $s = 0$, where $|X| = 2$.
What a zero does

A zero is the mirror image. Near it, $|X| \approx c' \cdot d$, a shallow funnel pointing down to the floor. In decibels the floor is minus infinity, so the viewer clips at $-30$ dB and a zero shows as a pit with a flat bottom. Zeros are where a signal's transform vanishes: the damped cosine $e^{-0.5t}\cos(1.5t)u(t)$ has $X(s) = (s+0.5)/((s+0.5)^2 + 2.25)$, with one zero at $s = -0.5$, and the same two poles as the damped sine. The zero sits on the real axis at the same $\sigma$ as the two poles, level with the middle of the pair. At $s = j1$ the zero distance is $1.118$ and the pole distances are the same $0.707$ and $2.55$, so $|X(j1)| = 1.118/1.803 = 0.620$.

The sine and the cosine therefore share poles, and so share the ringing, but differ in the numerator, and so differ in how much of each frequency they carry. At $\omega = 0$ the sine's height is $0.6$; the cosine's is $0.2$.
Decibels or magnitude?

The two height settings answer different questions. In decibels, $20\log_{10}|X|$ turns the product of distances into a sum, so every pole and zero adds its own contribution in a way you can stack. A 6 dB change is a factor of 2 in height, and a double pole counts twice. The range is $\pm 30$ dB, which is a factor of $0.032$ to $31.6$, so you can see both the deepest pit and the tallest peak at once. Zeros stay visible as pits.

In plain magnitude, the surface from 0 to 5 is the real thing, so a peak looks as sharp as it really is. A resonance with a height of 5 and a resonance with a height of 1 look very different here and similar in decibels. When you want to say \"how much\" use magnitude; when you want to see where poles and zeros are, use decibels.

Switch Height shows between decibels and magnitude with the damped sine selected, and compare the pole peaks. In magnitude the peaks are narrow spikes, cut off at the top of the box right next to the poles; in decibels they are broad hills that rise to about $20$ dB, two thirds of the way from the 0 dB middle to the top. Then switch the signal to damped cosine: a pit appears at $\sigma = -0.5$ on the real axis in decibels (the zero), where the sine has nothing.
Not every transform is rational

Two signals in the viewer are not ratios of polynomials. The delayed impulse has $X(s) = e^{-s}$, and the 3-second pulse has $X(s) = (1 - e^{-3s})/s$. For these, there is no ruler reading; the viewer says so. The pulse has infinitely many zeros, all on the imaginary axis at $\omega = 2\pi k/3$; the page A Gallery of Signals (#/math/laplace-transform/gallery) walks through it.
Problems

blocks.title: Measure a surface
blocks.text: A signal has $X(s) = 3/\bigl((s+1)(s+2)\bigr)$. What is $|X|$ at $s = j1$?
solution: The poles are at $-1$ and $-2$. The distance from $j1$ to $-1$ is $|1 + j1| = 1.414$. The distance from $j1$ to $-2$ is $|2 + j1| = 2.236$. So $|X(j1)| = 3/(1.414 \times 2.236) = 3/3.162 = 0.949$.

blocks.title: Where is the peak?
blocks.text: For $X(s) = 1.5/(s^2 + s + 2.5)$, show that the peak of $|X(j\omega)|$ on the imaginary axis is at $\omega = \sqrt{2}$ rad/s, and find its height.
solution: On the axis $|X|^2 = 2.25/\bigl((2.5 - \omega^2)^2 + \omega^2\bigr)$. The denominator is smallest when its derivative vanishes: $-4(2.5 - \omega^2)\omega + 2\omega = 0$, so $\omega^2 = 2.5 - 0.5 = 2$. At $\omega^2 = 2$ the denominator is $0.25 + 2 = 2.25$, so $|X|^2 = 1$.
The peak is at $\sqrt{2} = 1.414$, a little left of the pole's height $1.5$, and exactly $1$ high. It is pulled down from $1.5$ by the far pole.
